domain.title: Research Practice & Public Artifacts
domain.tag: read · reproduce · measure · write · publish · apply
domain.why: The engineers who make unusually fast jumps into top research labs almost all share one habit: they build things in public. That means writing up what you tried, publishing code, explaining what you learned — even when it's small. Top labs say this openly: public work is one of the strongest things you can show, often more convincing than a degree. This domain is also where you learn why Whetstone itself is built the way it is, so the tool you're using stops being a mystery too.

sections.note: Reading is a budgeted activity with a stopping rule, not an act of devotion.

L0.body:
# Keshav, How to Read a Paper (ACM SIGCOMM CCR 37(3), 2007)

pass 1  5-10 min  abstract, intro, headings, conclusions, refs
                  extract: Category, Context, Correctness, Contributions, Clarity
                  output:  a decision - stop, or continue

pass 2  <= 1 h    figures, tables, axes, units, error bars; the setup
                  skip proofs
                  output:  a summary with evidence, for someone else

pass 3  1-5 h     virtual re-implementation, from the same assumptions
                  output:  hidden assumptions; the experiment they skipped
L0.cloze: Keshav's first pass takes {{c1::5-10 minutes}} and its only output is {{c2::a decision to stop or continue}}. The third pass is a {{c3::virtual re-implementation}} and takes about {{c4::1-5 hours}}.

concepts.L1: Keshav's method: a 5-to-10 minute triage pass, a one-hour comprehension pass, and a one-to-five hour reconstruction pass. Each pass has a different output, and you enter the next one only if the previous one earned it.
concepts.L2: The passes are not increasing thoroughness applied to the same activity. They answer different questions. Pass one asks whether this paper is for you. Pass two asks what was actually measured. Pass three asks whether you would get the same number.
concepts.L3: Linear reading fails because comprehension is not uniform across a paper. Most of the decision-relevant content sits in the abstract, the figures and the experimental section; the related-work prose and the proofs carry almost none of it on a first encounter. Budgeting by pass converts an unbounded task into three bounded ones with explicit exit conditions, which is why you finish. It also matches how you will use the paper: most you need only at pass-one depth, a few at pass two, and one or two a month at pass three, which is the only depth from which you can reproduce anything or find an error.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {h} hours of reading time this week and {n} candidate papers. You pass-one every candidate (10 min each) and pass-two exactly half of them (60 min each). Using the remaining time at 180 min per pass-three read, how many papers reach pass three?
L4.answer: floor((60*h - 40*n) / 180). For h=20, n=8 that is floor(880/180) = 4; for h=10, n=8 it is floor(280/180) = 1; for h=40, n=12 it is floor(1920/180) = 10.
L4.explanation: Pass one costs 10n minutes, pass two costs 60 times n/2 which is 30n, so the fixed cost is 40n minutes. What is left of 60h minutes divides by 180. The point of the arithmetic is that pass three is expensive enough that a week buys single digits, which is why the stopping rule in pass one has to be real.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are {g} into a pass-two read and realise you cannot tell what the baseline was trained on. What do you do, and which pass does that question belong to?
L4.answer: Stop reading prose and go to the experimental section, appendix and released code, because 'what was the baseline trained on' is the core pass-two question. If the paper does not answer it, that is a finding about the paper: record it and either drop to pass one and move on, or escalate to pass three against the code.
L4.explanation: Pass two is defined by the experimental setup, not by the narrative. A setup you cannot reconstruct is the single most common reason a result fails to reproduce, and noticing it is worth more than finishing the paper.

L0.body:
# The read/skip decision, applied at the end of pass one.

read if:   it changes something you will do this month
           OR it is the load-bearing citation under a claim you rely on
           OR you intend to reproduce it

skip if:   you are reading it to feel current
           OR the abstract's claim is one you already believe and will not test
           OR no code, no released hyperparameters, and no error bars

queue:     one line in a notes file - title, url, why it might matter, date
           re-triage the queue monthly; unread after 90 days is a delete, not a debt
L0.cloze: The default answer at the end of pass one is {{c1::skip}}. Read only if the paper {{c2::changes something you will do this month}}, sits under a claim you rely on, or you intend to {{c3::reproduce}} it.

concepts.L1: The output of pass one is usually a decision to stop. A read/skip rule makes that explicit: read only if the paper changes an action, supports a claim you depend on, or is a reproduction target. Everything else goes in a queue with a expiry date.
concepts.L2: The failure is not reading too little, it is reading to feel current. Papers consumed for currency produce recognition, and recognition is the weakest memory format there is: Rowland's meta-analysis puts recognition tests at g around 0.31 against 0.5 to 0.8 for recall.
concepts.L3: arXiv cs.LG alone posts on the order of a hundred papers a day. No stopping rule means the queue wins, and the symptom is a person who can name every recent result and reproduce none of them. The rule to internalise is Catherine Olsson's: rather than learn X, try to learn to do X. A paper you will not act on, cite or reproduce is not learning material, it is news. Keep the queue anyway - a one-line entry costs seconds - but timestamp entries and delete rather than carry them. A queue that only grows is a to-do list that has become a guilt generator, which is the SRS review-backlog failure under another name.

L4.prompt_tpl: A paper claims a {p} percent improvement on a benchmark you do not use, releases no code, and reports a single run. Apply the read/skip rule and justify the call.
L4.answer: Skip, and record one line in the queue. It fails all three read conditions: it changes no action of yours, you do not depend on the claim, and with no code and one run it is not a viable reproduction target. A single run on a benchmark you do not use carries almost no information either way.
L4.explanation: The rule is deliberately harsh because the cost of a wrong skip is bounded - the paper still exists, and if it matters it will be cited at you - while the cost of a wrong read is an hour you cannot get back plus the illusion that you engaged with it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why keeping {n} unread papers in a queue is fine but keeping them as an obligation is not.
L4.answer: The queue is an index: a one-line entry costs seconds and makes the paper findable when a project actually needs it. Treating the same list as a backlog converts it into debt, produces avoidance, and the avoidance generalises to the whole practice. Timestamp entries and delete at 90 days.
L4.explanation: This is the same mechanism as the SRS review-debt spiral: an accumulating obligation triggers avoidance, avoidance grows the obligation. The fix in both cases is to make the store lossy on purpose rather than to promise yourself you will catch up.

concepts.t: Entry points and the call graph

L0.body:
# Reading an unfamiliar repo: find where control enters, then follow it down.

rg -n 'if __name__' --glob '!test*'        # python entry points
cat pyproject.toml | rg -A3 'scripts|console_scripts'
rg -n 'def main|argparse|@click|@app.command'

# then map the graph outward from one entry point, not inward from the file tree
python -X importtime -c 'import pkg' 2>&1 | tail -20     # what actually loads
python -m cProfile -s cumtime train.py --steps 1 | head -40   # what actually runs

# LOC is a map of the territory; the call graph is the territory.
L0.cloze: Start reading a repo from an {{c1::entry point}}, not the file tree. `python -m cProfile -s cumtime` sorted by {{c2::cumulative time}} gives you the call graph of what actually ran, which beats reading {{c3::directory listings}}.

concepts.L1: You do not read a codebase, you trace one execution of it. Find the entry point (a main, a console script, a test), run it once with the smallest possible input, and let the call graph tell you which of the thousands of files are on the path.
concepts.L2: Directory structure is documentation written by the authors for themselves and it is often a lie about importance. A profile sorted by cumulative time, or a single stack trace from a deliberately triggered exception, ranks the code by what actually executes.
concepts.L3: A large repo has a huge static surface and a small dynamic one. Of 400 files, a training run might touch 30, and 6 of those hold the logic you care about. Reading breadth-first from the file tree spends your attention proportional to the code that exists; reading from an entry point spends it proportional to the code that runs. Concretely: run the smallest end-to-end path (one training step, one test, one request), capture it with cProfile sorted by cumulative time or with py-spy, and you get a ranked list of the functions on the critical path. Then read those, in call order, top down. The same move works in C++ and Rust with perf and a debugger; the language changes, the principle does not.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are handed a {n}-file research repo and asked to change how the loss is computed. Give the first three commands you run and say why the file tree is not one of them.
L4.answer: Find the entry point (rg for __main__ or console_scripts), run the smallest end-to-end step under cProfile or py-spy, and grep the profile output for loss. The file tree ranks by the authors' filing habits; the profile ranks by execution, which is what a change to the loss actually intersects.
L4.explanation: The static surface and the dynamic surface of a repo differ by an order of magnitude. Any strategy that reads in file-tree order pays attention proportional to the wrong quantity, and in a research repo much of the static surface is dead experiment code.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague says they have read the whole repo and still cannot find where the {thing} is applied. What is wrong with their method?
L4.answer: They read statically, so they never learned which of the several definitions is the one that runs. Research repos routinely contain three implementations of a thing, two of them dead. A single run with a breakpoint or a print at the call site resolves in seconds what static reading cannot resolve at all.
L4.explanation: Dead code is the normal state of a research repository, because experiments are kept rather than deleted. Only execution distinguishes the live definition from the abandoned ones, which is why the debugger is a reading tool and not just a fixing tool.

L0.body:
# The debugger as a reading tool: stop at the line, inspect the world.
(Pdb) b model.py:214 ; c ; pp {k: v.shape for k, v in batch.items()} ; w ; u

# git as the record of why the code is shaped like this
git log -L 200,260:model.py       # history of just these lines
git log -S 'rotary_emb' --oneline # commits that added or removed the string
git blame -w -C -M model.py       # ignore whitespace, follow moves and copies
git bisect start HEAD v0.3.1      # find the commit that changed the number
git log --merges --oneline -20    # which PRs; then read those threads
L0.cloze: `git log -S` finds commits where a {{c1::string's occurrence count changed}}, `git log -L` shows the history of {{c2::a line range}}, and `git blame -w -C -M` ignores whitespace and follows {{c3::code that moved or was copied}}.

concepts.L1: Two reading tools most people only use for fixing. A breakpoint answers what the data actually looks like at line 214; git log -S, git log -L and git blame answer why the line is there and what it replaced.
concepts.L2: git blame without -w -C -M lies to you constantly: a reformat or a file move makes every line look authored by whoever ran the formatter. The commit message is usually worthless; the linked PR discussion is where the reasoning is.
concepts.L3: Code carries no record of the alternatives tried and rejected, and that is precisely what you need in order to change it safely. History carries it. A one-line workaround commented 'temp fix' is meaningless until git log -S on the surrounding symbol shows it landed the same day as a revert and the PR thread names the failing case. A breakpoint is the fastest reading instrument available: actual tensor shapes, dtypes and device placement in a research codebase are almost never what the hints and docstrings claim. Ten seconds at a breakpoint resolves what ten minutes of reading leaves ambiguous. git bisect turns 'when did this number change' into a logarithmic search you can automate.

L4.prompt_tpl: A regression appeared somewhere in the last {n} commits. Each bisect step costs {m} minutes to build and test. What is the worst-case wall-clock cost of git bisect, and how does that compare with reading all {n} diffs? Answer with the worst-case bisect cost in minutes.
L4.answer: ceil(log2(n)) * m minutes. For n=512, m=4 that is 9*4 = 36 minutes; n=1024, m=4 is 10*4 = 40; n=512, m=9 is 81. Reading n diffs at even one minute each is 512 to 1024 minutes.
L4.explanation: Bisect is binary search over commits, so the cost is logarithmic in history length and linear in the cost of one test. That is why the highest-leverage preparation is a fast scripted reproducer: git bisect run turns the whole search into one command.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why `git blame` on a file that was reformatted {t} shows almost no useful authorship, and which flags fix it.
L4.answer: A wholesale reformat rewrites every line, so blame attributes all of them to the formatting commit. -w ignores whitespace-only changes, -C detects lines copied from other files in the same commit, and -M detects lines moved within a file. Together they see through the reformat to the real authoring commit.
L4.explanation: Blame is a per-line last-touch index, not an authorship record. Every mechanical rewrite - formatters, license headers, import sorters, mass renames - destroys it unless you ask blame to look through them.

L0.body:
# ACM's terms (Artifact Review and Badging v1.1), which the ML community mostly ignores.

repeatable    same team, same artifact, same setup          -> you rerun your own code
reproducible  different team, SAME artifact (their code)    -> you run their code
replicable    different team, DIFFERENT artifact (your code) -> you rewrite it

# NeurIPS/ICML usage inverts 'reproducible' and 'replicable' relative to ACM.
# Say what you did, not which word you used:
#   'ran the released code on the released config, got 71.2 vs 71.4 reported, 3 seeds'
L0.cloze: Under ACM's badging terms, running {{c1::their code}} is reproduction and rewriting it as {{c2::your own implementation}} is replication - and the ML literature routinely {{c3::swaps the two words}}, so state what you actually did instead.

concepts.L1: Three distinct things get called reproduction: rerunning your own artifact, running someone else's artifact, and rebuilding the result from the paper alone. They test different claims and have wildly different costs.
concepts.L2: The words are not stable. ACM and the ML conferences use reproducible and replicable in opposite senses, so the label communicates nothing. Report the operation instead: whose code, whose data, whose hyperparameters, how many seeds, and what number you got.
concepts.L3: Each level falsifies something different. Running their code and failing means the artifact is broken or the environment underspecified. Running your own implementation and failing means either you are wrong or the paper omits something load-bearing, and you cannot tell which until you diff against their code. That asymmetry is why the order is reproduce first, replicate second: their artifact is your oracle. Gundersen and Kjensmo's survey of AAAI and IJCAI papers found only a small minority shared code and data, which is why many reproductions start at the hardest level. The most useful sentence in a write-up is operational: which artifact, which config, how many seeds, what you got.

L4.prompt_tpl: You reimplement a paper from the text and get {d} points below the reported number. Name the two hypotheses this is consistent with, and the cheapest experiment that separates them.
L4.answer: Either your implementation differs from theirs, or the paper omits something load-bearing. Cheapest separator: run their released code on their config. If it hits the reported number, the gap is in your code and you diff. If it does not, the gap is in the paper or the environment and you have found something publishable.
L4.explanation: Failure at the replication level is uninformative on its own because two very different causes produce the same symptom. Reproduction with the authors' artifact is the oracle that splits them, which is why you do it first even when your goal is a from-scratch implementation.

L4.prompt_tpl: A write-up says 'we reproduced the result'. List the {n} facts that sentence must be expanded into before it means anything.
L4.answer: Whose code, whose data and preprocessing, whose hyperparameters and config, how many seeds and what spread, and on what hardware and software versions. Plus the number you obtained against the number reported.
L4.explanation: 'Reproduced' is a claim about a process, and the process is exactly what the word hides. Papers with Reproducibility badges attach these facts as an artifact appendix precisely because the adjective alone is not checkable.

L0.body:
# Shrink until the result appears in seconds, then keep it there.

target:   one file, one command, under 5 minutes on one GPU (ideally on CPU)
          fixed seed, tiny model, tiny data slice, assert on the number

# example skeleton
python repro.py --steps 200 --d_model 64 --n_layer 2 --seed 0
  step 200 | loss 4.812 | expected 4.81 +/- 0.05   OK

# the test is: does the PHENOMENON survive the shrink, not the absolute number.
# if the effect disappears at small scale, that is itself the finding - report it.
L0.cloze: A minimal reproduction is {{c1::one file, one command}}, runs in minutes, and asserts on the number. The thing that must survive shrinking is {{c2::the phenomenon}}, not the absolute metric value.

concepts.L1: A minimal reproduction is the smallest self-contained script that exhibits the phenomenon, with a fixed seed and an assertion on the expected value. It is the unit of currency in experimental work: it is what you debug, share, and file bugs against.
concepts.L2: Minimal does not mean simplified. Every element you strip must be one you have shown the effect does not depend on. Stripping until it runs fast and then finding the effect is gone tells you nothing unless you checked at each step which removal killed it.
concepts.L3: A minimal repro converts a slow, noisy, expensive question into a fast, deterministic, cheap one, and that changes what you are able to do. At five minutes a run you can bisect, ablate and try twenty variants in an afternoon; at six hours a run you get one guess a day and you will start rationalising instead of testing. The construction is a bisection over the configuration: halve the model, halve the data, halve the steps, and after each cut check the phenomenon is still there. When it disappears you have localised a dependency, which is a result. Karpathy's recipe works from the other end - dumbest end-to-end skeleton, fixed seeds, verify the initial loss matches theory, then add.

L4.prompt_tpl: A run takes {t} hours. You shrink it to a {m}-minute minimal repro. In one 8-hour day, how many hypotheses can you test in each regime, and what is the ratio? Answer with the ratio.
L4.answer: floor(8/t) versus floor(480/m). For t=6, m=5: 1 versus 96, a ratio of 96. For t=3, m=12: 2 versus 40, a ratio of 20. For t=6, m=12: 1 versus 40.
L4.explanation: The ratio is the whole argument. Iteration count, not cleverness, is what finds the bug, and shrinking the loop by one to two orders of magnitude changes the kind of question you are able to ask - from one guess a day to a systematic sweep.

L4.prompt_tpl: Someone shrinks a repro from {a} layers to {b} and the effect vanishes, so they conclude their minimal repro is broken. What is the error in that reasoning?
L4.answer: The effect vanishing is data, not a bug. It says the phenomenon depends on something they removed - depth, capacity, or a training-duration threshold. The correct move is to bisect the cut to find the smallest configuration where it survives, and report that threshold as part of the result.
L4.explanation: Treating a disappearing effect as a broken harness discards the most informative observation available: the boundary of the phenomenon. Many published findings are really claims about a regime, and the shrink is what locates the regime's edge.

L0.body:
# Four rungs. Each one is publishable. Each one costs about 3x the last.

1 rerun       their code, their config, their data   -> does the artifact work?
2 reimplement your code, their config, their data   -> is the paper sufficient?
3 vary        your code, new seeds/data/scale/hparams -> how far does it hold?
4 extend      a claim the paper implies but never tested -> a contribution

# Stop where your evidence stops. A clean rung 2 write-up beats a hand-waved rung 4.
L0.cloze: The ladder runs rerun, {{c1::reimplement}}, vary, {{c2::extend}}. Rung 3 asks how far the claim holds under {{c3::new conditions}} such as different seeds, data or scale.

concepts.L1: Rerun their artifact, reimplement from the paper, vary the conditions, extend to a claim they did not test. Four rungs, each roughly three times the cost of the last, and each one a complete artifact you can publish on its own.
concepts.L2: Most people jump to rung four because it sounds like research, and produce something unfalsifiable. Rungs one and two are where the errors live, and a negative result at rung two - the paper is not sufficient to rebuild the result - is a genuine contribution that gets read.
concepts.L3: The ladder is ordered by how much of the uncertainty is yours. At rung one any failure is theirs. At rung two failure is ambiguous until you diff against their code, which is why rung one comes first. At rung three you begin to own the claim: the standard variations are seeds, dataset, scale and tuning budget, and the standard finding is that a headline gap shrinks or inverts under one of them - Melis, Dyer and Blunsom found properly regularised LSTMs beat newer architectures once every model got equal tuning. Rung four is where a reproduction becomes a paper, and it is reachable because rungs one to three taught you the failure modes of the setup.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {w} weeks and no prior publications. Pick a rung to target and justify it against the alternative one rung higher.
L4.answer: Target rung two, and a clean rung three if it comes cheaply. A finished reimplementation with released code, seed spread and an honest diff against the paper is a complete artifact; a half-finished extension is not an artifact at all. Cost roughly triples per rung, so one rung up is most of the budget.
L4.explanation: Finishing is the constraint that dominates. The ladder exists so that you can stop at a rung and still have shipped something legible, which is exactly what a first public artifact needs to be.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why a rung-{r} result that contradicts the paper is more valuable to publish than a rung-{r} result that confirms it.
L4.answer: Confirmation is the prior; the literature already asserts it, so the update is small. A contradiction is a large update and is scarce, because negative results are systematically under-published. It also forces you to be precise about the conditions, which is where the real content is.
L4.explanation: The caveat is that a contradiction has a much higher evidential bar: before publishing it you must have run their artifact, matched their preprocessing, and reported seed spread, or you have published your own bug.

L0.body:
# What a hiring reader can verify in five minutes:

  a repo that runs           -> you can ship
  a number that matches      -> you can measure
  a documented divergence    -> you are honest under pressure
  a seed spread and CI       -> you know what a result is
  a written-up decision log  -> you can communicate

# What they cannot verify: a course certificate, a reading list, a grade.
# Anthropic careers: 'interesting independent research, thoughtful blog posts,
#  or open source contributions'. Neel Nanda: 'public research output is your
#  best credential.'
L0.cloze: A reproduction is legible because a reader can check {{c1::the number against the paper}} in minutes. Anthropic's careers page asks for independent research, blog posts or {{c2::open source contributions}} rather than credentials.

concepts.L1: A reproduction is the highest-signal-per-hour artifact available to someone with no track record, because it is externally checkable. The claim has a reference value, the code either runs or does not, and the reader needs no trust in you at all.
concepts.L2: It is not valued because reproducing is hard. It is valued because it is falsifiable. A from-scratch side project proves only that you can build something nobody will check; a reproduction puts a number next to a published number and invites the comparison.
concepts.L3: The four inputs common to every documented fast transition: a strong foundation, full-time focus, a named mentor or feedback community, and an environment producing public artifacts by default. Reproduction is the cheapest way to manufacture the fourth alone. Ziegler's route into OpenAI's safety team was six weeks of reimplementing five or more foundational deep-RL algorithms at two to ten days each - rung two, repeated. The EleutherAI paper records people with minimal CS background becoming core contributors within weeks, where work was public by construction. The honesty: Ziegler was an MIT CS graduate who had begun a Stanford PhD, so those weeks were retargeting.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {h} hours and want one artifact for a fellowship application. Choose between a novel side project and a reproduction with an ablation, and justify on verifiability.
L4.answer: The reproduction. Its claim is checkable against a published reference number in minutes, so it transfers signal without requiring the reader to trust your framing. A novel project makes the reader evaluate both the problem choice and the execution, which is a much higher bar with no external anchor.
L4.explanation: Reviewers are time-constrained and default to skepticism about unverifiable claims. An artifact whose correctness a stranger can check cheaply converts your effort into evidence; one that cannot is asking for trust you have not yet earned.

L4.prompt_tpl: Ziegler moved from software engineering into OpenAI's safety team after about {w} weeks. Explain what that number does and does not support.
L4.answer: It supports the claim that reimplementation is an efficient route into research engineering: he read 20 to 30 deep-RL papers and implemented five or more algorithms at 2 to 10 days each. It does not support 'novice to OpenAI in six weeks': he had an MIT CS degree, had started a Stanford PhD, and was already an elite engineer retargeting existing ability.
L4.explanation: The 80,000 Hours guide states its own assumed starting point - a technical degree plus the ability to pass a Google software interview - and gives a floor of at minimum 200 hours for someone starting with less. Quoting the six weeks without the fine print is the standard misuse of this case.

concepts.L1: An ablation removes one component to attribute the effect to it. It only works if removal changes nothing else - and removal always changes parameter count, compute, and often the optimal learning rate, so those have to be re-matched.
concepts.L2: The standard broken ablation deletes a module and keeps everything else literally identical, which quietly compares a bigger model against a smaller one at the same step count. The finding then reads as 'more parameters help', dressed up as a claim about the component.
concepts.L3: Three things move when you ablate. Parameters and FLOPs drop, so widen or deepen what remains until the budgets agree. The loss landscape changes, so the previously tuned learning rate is no longer optimal for the ablated arm - and an undertuned arm loses, which is the artefact Melis and colleagues found once every model got equal tuning. Regularisation interacts, so a module that also regularises cannot be removed without re-tuning dropout and weight decay. The defensible protocol: match parameters and token budget, tune the learning rate independently per arm over the same grid, run several seeds, report the interval. Anything less measures your tuning effort, not the component.

L4.prompt_tpl: Removing a module drops params from {a}M to {b}M and val accuracy by 1.2 points, and the authors conclude the module is essential. State the flaw and the fix.

L4.explanation: Seeds are what convert a number into an estimate with an interval. Spending your budget on more conditions measured badly maximises the number of claims you cannot defend, which is the opposite of what a limited budget should buy.

#   from top venues, systematically re-evaluated.

  reproducible with reasonable effort ..... 7 of 18   (39%)

  consistently better than a tuned linear . 0

#   SEED, can show an apparently significant difference against itself.
# NeurIPS response: code-submission policy + the ML Reproducibility Checklist.
L0.cloze: Dacrema and colleagues could reproduce {{c1::7}} of 18 neural recommender papers, and {{c2::6}} of those were beaten by simple heuristics. Henderson showed the same algorithm split by {{c3::seed}} can look significantly different from itself.

concepts.L1: ML has a reproducibility problem distinct from psychology's. Very little is fraud. The mechanism is underspecified setups, uncontrolled variance, unlogged hyperparameter search, and unreleased code, combined with a reviewing culture that rewarded the number.
concepts.L2: The crisis is not that results are false, it is that most published numbers are the maximum over an unreported search. Max over n trials rises with n regardless of method quality, so a paper with more compute for tuning wins even when its method is neutral.
concepts.L3: Dacrema and colleagues re-evaluated 18 neural recommendation papers from top venues: only 7 could be reproduced with reasonable effort, and 6 of those 7 were often beaten by simple nearest-neighbour or graph heuristics. Henderson and colleagues showed that in deep RL the between-seed variance is large enough that one algorithm can appear significantly different from itself. The response was structural rather than moral: NeurIPS added a code-submission policy and the ML Reproducibility Checklist, ACM added artifact badging. The consequence for you: the base rate of claims surviving an honest reimplementation is low enough that a careful reproduction is a contribution.

L4.prompt_tpl: Of {n} papers, {r} were reproducible with reasonable effort, and {b} of those were often beaten by simple heuristics. What fraction of the original {n} survived as clear improvements over simple baselines?
L4.answer: (r - b)/n = (7-6)/18 = 1/18, about 5.6 percent. And the paper notes that the one survivor did not consistently beat a well-tuned linear ranking method either.
L4.explanation: The arithmetic is the point. Two independent filters - can it be rebuilt, and does it beat something simple - each remove most of the field, and they compose multiplicatively. This is the base rate you should hold when reading any single new result.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why 'report the best of {k} runs' is a reporting practice that manufactures progress with no dishonesty on anyone's part.
L4.answer: The maximum of k draws from any distribution increases with k, so a method given a larger search budget reports a higher number regardless of quality. Nobody lied; the statistic itself is budget-dependent. The fix is Dodge's: report expected best performance as a function of search budget, so the comparison is budget-matched.
L4.explanation: This is why compute-rich groups can appear to make faster methodological progress than they do, and why a reproduction that matches tuning budget across arms often erases a published gap without finding any error in the original.

concepts.L2: You cannot fix this by trying harder to be fair, because the asymmetry is structural: you debug your method until it works and you stop debugging the baseline as soon as it runs. The only fix is a budget-matched protocol fixed before you start.
concepts.L3: Two large studies make this concrete. concepts.L1: Every metric is a proxy for something you cannot measure directly. Optimising against it moves the proxy and the target apart, because the cheapest way to raise the proxy is almost never the thing the proxy was standing in for.
concepts.L2: The second, quieter error is treating statistical significance as importance. concepts.L3: The decoupling has a mechanism. A metric is a function of behaviour with a large preimage: many behaviours produce the same score, and only some are the behaviour you wanted. Optimisation searches that preimage and finds the cheapest member, usually a shortcut - length bias in preference scores, formatting bias in judged evaluations, n-gram matching in BLEU. The defences: hold out a metric you never optimise against, rotate evaluations, read samples by hand, report effect sizes with intervals rather than p-values. Significance answers whether the sign is reliable; effect size answers whether anyone should care. State the effect in the units the reader pays in.

# Write the kill condition at the start, in the same file as the hypothesis.

            OR the minimal repro will not stabilise

            OR someone published it last week and did it better

concepts.L2: The failure is not persisting too long, it is abandoning silently. A project you quietly stop leaves nothing behind, so you cannot tell later whether the idea was wrong or your implementation was, and neither can anyone else who tries it next.
concepts.L3: Sunk cost is the obvious trap, and the standard advice - hours already spent are not evidence about hours remaining - is correct but insufficient, because the real driver is that abandoning feels like admitting the time was wasted. L4.explanation: The instability, not the missing signal, is the decisive fact. Without a stable repro every subsequent result is uninterpretable, so the project has no path to a defensible claim regardless of how much time remains.

# One claim. Everything below it is evidence or context for that claim.

  title      the claim, or the specific thing you did. not a topic.
  first 3 lines   what you did, what you found, why it matters. no throat-clearing.
  the result      the number or the figure, early. before the method.
  how            enough for a reader to rebuild it. link the repo.
  what it means   the interpretation, clearly separated from the result.
  limitations     what you did not test. this is where credibility is won.

# Headings must be readable alone, in order, as a summary of the post.
L0.cloze: A technical post carries {{c1::one claim}}. Put the result {{c2::before the method}}, and write headings that read alone, in order, as a {{c3::summary of the post}}.

concepts.L1: One claim per post, stated in the title and in the first three lines, with the result before the method. Then how you did it, what it means, and what you did not test. Limitations are not a formality; they are where a technical reader decides to trust you.
concepts.L2: Nobody reads linearly. A technical reader scans the title, the first paragraph, the figures and the headings, and decides in about fifteen seconds whether to read. So the structure has to survive being skimmed: the headings alone must tell the story, and every figure must be legible with only its caption.
concepts.L3: Writing result-first inverts the order in which you did the work, and that is the point: your order is chronological, the reader's is importance-ordered. Rachel Thomas sharpens the targeting - pick one specific reader, and write about what you learned last month, because you are best positioned to help the person one step behind you and you still remember what was confusing. Olah and Carter's Research Debt makes the structural argument: unclear explanation is a cost the whole field pays, and distillation is research work, not a service task. The test before publishing: delete every sentence that does not support the one claim, then check the headings still read as a summary.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have a post with {n} sections that opens with {k} paragraphs of background before the result. Rewrite the opening in outline form and justify the reordering.
L4.answer: Open with the claim and the number in three lines, then one short paragraph of context only if the claim is unintelligible without it, then the figure. Background moves below the result or into a link. The reason is that the reader decides whether to continue before reaching paragraph three, so anything load-bearing must be above that line.
L4.explanation: This is the inverted-pyramid structure from news writing, and it works for the same reason: readers leave at every paragraph boundary, so information should be ordered by importance rather than by the order in which you discovered it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain the test 'read only the {n} headings in order' and what a failure of that test tells you about the draft.
L4.answer: If the headings alone do not convey the claim, the evidence and the conclusion, the post relies on the reader consuming every paragraph, which most will not do. Failure usually means the headings are topics rather than statements: 'Results' instead of 'Rotary embeddings cut val loss by 0.05 at fixed compute'.
L4.explanation: Turning headings into assertions is the cheapest structural upgrade available to a draft. It also exposes missing structure, because a section with no assertion to make is usually a section that should be a sentence.

# A figure must be readable with only its caption, by someone who read nothing else.

  error bars or a shaded band, and the caption says what they are (sd? 95% CI? n?)
  the baseline on the same axes, not in a different figure
  the caption states the takeaway as a sentence, not 'Figure 3: results'

#   'Fig 3. Method B reaches the same val loss as A using 38% fewer FLOPs.
#    5 seeds per arm, shaded band is +/- 1 sd, iso-FLOP budget, 124M params.'

concepts.L1: The figure is the part of your write-up that most readers will actually consume, so it has to carry the argument alone. Labelled axes with units, the baseline on the same axes, an error band whose definition is stated, and a caption that says what to conclude.
concepts.L2: A figure without an error band is a claim without evidence, and the most common tell of an unreliable result. The second tell is a caption that names the figure instead of stating the finding, which signals the author has not decided what the figure is for.

Practical rules: same axes for compared arms, compute rather than steps on the x-axis when the claim is about efficiency, a log axis when the quantity spans orders of magnitude and say so, and never two bars without intervals.

L4.answer: No uncertainty shown, so the difference cannot be assessed; no n; no statement of what varies between arms; and a caption that names rather than concludes. L4.explanation: Two bars without intervals is the single most common uninformative figure in applied ML. It is not merely incomplete: it actively invites the reader to treat a difference of unknown reliability as a fact.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are claiming a {p} percent efficiency win. Explain why the x-axis should be compute rather than training steps.
L4.answer: Steps are not a cost. Plotting against FLOPs or wall-clock makes the claim mean what it says.
L4.explanation: The general rule for efficiency claims is that the x-axis must be the resource you claim to be saving. Anything else lets the comparison drift away from the sentence in the abstract.

  1 context     one sentence a non-specialist in your subfield can follow
  2 the gap     what was not known or not tested
  3 what we did the method, in one sentence, concrete
  4 the result  the number, with its condition ('at equal compute', '5 seeds')
  5 so what     what a reader should now do or believe differently

# A claim with no figure is either unsupported or belongs in future work.
L0.cloze: Test the abstract by naming, for each claim, {{c1::the figure or table that supports it}}. A claim with no supporting evidence belongs in {{c2::future work}}, not the abstract.

concepts.L1: The abstract is the only part most readers see, and every clause in it is a promise the body must pay. The test is mechanical: for each claim, name the figure or table that supports it, and delete or demote any claim with no answer.
concepts.L2: The common failure is not overclaiming in an obvious way, it is unconditioned claiming. 'Our method improves accuracy by 2 points' is a different, much stronger claim than 'by 2 points at equal compute on one benchmark over five seeds', and only the second is one you can defend.
concepts.L3: Nanda's advice is that a paper makes one to three specific concrete claims and everything else supports that narrative; the abstract is where you commit. The five-part structure - context, gap, method, result, implication - is a checklist, and its value is that a missing part is diagnostic. No gap means you have not said why the work was needed. No conditioned number means the result is not yet a result. No implication means you have not decided who this is for. Write the abstract before the paper is finished and rewrite it after: the first draft tells you what to run, the second what you found. The gap between them is the project's honest content.

L4.explanation: Running the name-the-figure test on your own abstract usually deletes one clause, and that deletion is the single highest-value edit in the paper, because unsupported abstract claims are what reviewers and readers punish hardest.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why writing the abstract {w} is a useful planning technique, not just a writing one.
L4.answer: The draft abstract states the result you hope for, which immediately names the experiments and figures required to support it - it is a work plan in disguise. Rewriting it afterwards against what you actually measured exposes exactly where your expectations and your evidence diverged, which is usually the most interesting part of the project.
L4.explanation: This is the same mechanism as writing the numeric prediction before a run: committing to a claim in advance makes the mismatch visible instead of letting the narrative quietly reshape itself around whatever happened.

L0.body:
# arXiv
  endorsement: a first-time submitter to a category may need an endorser,
    who checks topical fit only. It is explicitly NOT peer review.
  versions are permanent: v1 stays public forever. cross-list, never duplicate.
  pick a licence deliberately; the default is non-exclusive distribution.

# reviewer comments: sort every review into three bins
  1 wrong about the paper  -> your writing failed; fix the writing
  2 right and fixable      -> fix it, say so in the response
  3 right and not fixable  -> concede it in limitations
# 'they did not read it' is bin 1 until proven otherwise.
L0.cloze: arXiv endorsement checks only that a paper is {{c1::appropriate for the subject area}} and is explicitly not {{c2::peer review}}. A reviewer who misread your paper is evidence of {{c3::a writing failure}} until proven otherwise.

concepts.L1: arXiv is a preprint server with an endorsement gate for first-time submitters to a category, permanent versions and a licence choice. Peer review happens elsewhere. Reviewer comments sort into three bins: they misread you, they are right and it is fixable, they are right and it is not.
concepts.L2: Endorsement is not review and confers no quality signal; it only checks topical fit. And the reviewer who misunderstood your paper is data about your writing, not about the reviewer, because the next hundred readers will have less patience and no obligation.
concepts.L3: Treating misreadings as writing bugs is the highest-leverage habit in revision, because it is the only interpretation that produces an action. A reviewer who thought your baseline was untuned has told you the tuning protocol was not visible enough; move it into the main text. Practically: post to arXiv when the work is finished enough that you would defend it, remember v1 is permanent, cross-list rather than resubmit, pick a licence that permits the reuse you want. In the response letter, answer every point, concede plainly where you are wrong, never argue about tone. Conceding a real limitation raises credibility more than defending it could.

L4.prompt_tpl: A reviewer writes that your method is {c}, which is not what the paper says. Classify the comment and give your two actions.

c: an unmodified reimplementation of prior work

L4.answer: Bin one: they misread, which means the paper did not make it clear. Actions: change the text or a figure so the point is unmissable in the main body, and in the response say plainly what the paper does and point to the revised location. Do not merely assert that the reviewer was wrong.
L4.explanation: The response letter is read by an editor and by the reviewer, but the revised paper is read by everyone else. Fixing the writing serves both, and it is the only response that improves the artifact rather than the argument about it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain what arXiv endorsement does and does not certify, and why treating {t} as validation is a mistake.
L4.answer: Endorsement certifies that a submission is topically appropriate for a category, checked by an established author in that area. It certifies nothing about correctness, novelty or quality, and arXiv states it is not peer review. Treating a preprint as validated confuses distribution with evaluation.
L4.explanation: This matters in both directions: do not oversell your own preprint as a publication, and do not dismiss preprints as unreviewed noise, since much of the field's most-used work appears there first and is evaluated by reproduction rather than by review.

# The actual mechanism, in order. Each arrow has a failure mode.

  artifact -> found     needs: a real title, a searchable problem, readers
  found    -> read      needs: result first, figures, a claim in 3 lines
  read     -> reply     needs: something specific to disagree with
  reply    -> relation  needs: you answer, follow up, do the next thing
  relation -> referral  needs: someone who knows your work when a role opens

# Anthropic: 'We care about what you can do, not where you learned to do it.'
# levels.fyi on Distinguished engineers: 'frequently published authors'.
L0.cloze: The chain runs artifact, found, read, {{c1::reply}}, relationship, {{c2::referral}}. The step people neglect is making the artifact {{c3::specific enough to disagree with}}.

concepts.L1: Public work converts into opportunity through a chain: the artifact is found, read, replied to, and the reply becomes a relationship that later produces a referral. Every step has a distinct requirement, and the chain breaks at whichever one you neglect.
concepts.L2: The unintuitive requirement is at the reply step. A post that is agreeable and general gets read and forgotten; a post that makes a specific, falsifiable claim gets corrected, and being corrected in public by someone competent is the fastest path to knowing them.
concepts.L3: Three sources converge on public output as a credential. Neel Nanda: public research output is your best credential. Anthropic's careers page asks for independent research, thoughtful blog posts or open-source contributions, and states about half its technical staff had no prior ML experience. levels.fyi notes distinguished engineers are frequently published authors. The causal arrow in the last is ambiguous - senior people write and writers get senior - so treat it as weaker evidence than the fellowship data. What is not ambiguous is the individual mechanism: a referral needs someone who already knows what you can do.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your post got {v} views and no replies. Diagnose which link in the chain broke and give a concrete fix.
L4.answer: Reading happened, engagement did not, so the break is read-to-reply: the post gave nobody anything specific to argue with or build on. Fix: state a falsifiable claim with a number and a condition, name the limitation you are least sure about, and ask one precise question at the end.
L4.explanation: An open, specific question is the cheapest conversion device available and it is almost always omitted. It also signals that you want correction, which is what makes competent people willing to spend their time replying.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are based {loc} and targeting a lab whose research roles are all in SF and London. Argue for public artifacts over internal visibility as the primary strategy.
L4.answer: Internal visibility is structurally allocated to people near where decisions are made, so it is the weakest lever available to you. Public artifacts are location-independent and are read by exactly the people who staff those roles, which is why the fellowship and open-source routes dominate for remote candidates. The relocation or visa question remains live and should be planned, not deferred.
L4.explanation: Larson's survey found visibility to be structural - headquarters staff get more of it - and the labs' own job boards concentrate research roles in a few cities. Public work routes around the first constraint but does not remove the second.

# Pick a project you already use and can run the tests of.
  signals: merged PRs from non-maintainers this month; a CONTRIBUTING file;
           open labelled good-first-issues; maintainers who reply

# The first PR, in order:
  1 reproduce the bug and add a failing test
  2 smallest possible fix; no drive-by refactors; match local style
  3 one PR, one change; describe the failing case
  4 answer review within a day; ask, do not defend

# Leaderboards: GPU MODE runs kernel problems with a public leaderboard
#   (kernelbot); modded-nanogpt logs attributed speedrun records.
L0.cloze: A first PR should start with {{c1::a failing test}} that reproduces the bug, make the {{c2::smallest possible fix}}, and avoid {{c3::drive-by refactors}}.

concepts.L1: Contribute to something you already use and can run the tests of. The first PR is a failing test plus the smallest fix, one change, described by its failing case. Kernel leaderboards such as GPU MODE's are the same funnel with an automatic, comparable score attached.
concepts.L2: The reason first PRs stall is almost never the code. It is scope: a fix bundled with a refactor forces the maintainer to review two things and take responsibility for a design decision they did not ask for, so the cheapest response is to leave it.
concepts.L3: Maintainer time is the scarce resource, and PR etiquette follows from minimising your draw on it. A failing test proves the bug without them reproducing it. A minimal diff makes review cheap. One change per PR stops a disagreement about one part blocking the rest. Fast, non-defensive replies keep the PR from going cold, which is how most first contributions die. Repeat this and your PRs get read first, which is the start of the maintainer path - triage, review rights, commit. Leaderboards compress the same funnel: the artifact and its ranking arrive together and need no advocacy from you.

L4.prompt_tpl: A first-time contributor opens a PR with a {n}-line diff that fixes a bug, renames {k} variables for clarity, and reformats the file. It goes unreviewed for a month. Explain why, and rewrite the plan.
L4.answer: The diff mixes a fix with two unrequested changes, so the maintainer must evaluate a bug fix, a naming decision and a reformat at once, and the reformat hides the real change. Rewrite as one PR: a failing test plus the minimal fix. Propose the rename and the reformat separately, after the fix lands.
L4.explanation: Review cost scales with the number of independent decisions, not with lines changed. A one-decision PR can be approved in minutes; a three-decision PR needs a conversation the maintainer has to schedule, which is why it waits.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {h} hours and no public track record. Compare a leaderboard kernel submission with a first PR to a library you use, on speed of signal and durability.
L4.answer: The leaderboard gives faster, unambiguous signal: your score is comparable and attributed with no maintainer in the loop, so the result does not depend on anyone's availability. The merged PR is slower and gated on review, but it is durable evidence of working inside someone else's codebase, which is closer to the actual job. Do the leaderboard first, then the PR.
L4.explanation: They measure different things. A leaderboard rank shows you can optimise against a clear objective; a merged PR shows you can operate under constraints you did not choose, which is the harder and more transferable claim.

# Dunlosky 2013 rated 10 techniques for GENERALIZABILITY. Two got High:
  practice testing      High
  distributed practice  High
  everything else       Moderate or Low (rereading, highlighting: Low)

# Donoghue & Hattie 2021, effect sizes d (k studies):
  distributed practice 0.85 (k=150)   re-reading    0.47 (k=113)
  practice testing     0.74 (k=374)   interleaving  0.47 (k=104)
  self-explanation     0.54 (k=93)    summarization 0.44 (k=234)

# Cepeda 2008: the optimal gap gave a 64% increase in final recall over a
#   zero-day gap, at retention intervals of 7, 35, 70 and 350 days.
L0.cloze: Dunlosky rated only {{c1::practice testing}} and {{c2::distributed practice}} as high utility. Donoghue and Hattie put distributed practice at d = {{c3::0.85}} and practice testing at d = 0.74.

concepts.L1: Of ten studied techniques only two earn high utility ratings across learners, materials and criterion tasks: practice testing and distributed practice. Everything else is a supporting move. This is why the app schedules retrieval over time rather than presenting material.
concepts.L2: The ratings are about generalizability, not effect size, and the distinction matters: every technique in the 2021 meta-analysis clears d = 0.40, including re-reading at 0.47. What separates the top two is that they work across ages, materials and test formats, not that they are alone in working.
concepts.L3: Cepeda and colleagues ran 1,354 subjects across 26 gap-by-retention-interval combinations, at retention intervals of 7, 35, 70 and 350 days. The optimal gap produced a 64 percent increase in final recall over a zero-day gap. The optimum is not a fixed ratio: it falls from roughly 14 to 31 percent of the retention interval at a week to two months, to about 6 to 7 percent at a year. The curve rises steeply and declines gently, so over-spacing is cheap and under-spacing expensive. Against Macnamara's finding that in professions practice explains under 1 percent of performance variance: scheduling buys retention, not expertise.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to still know something in {r} days. Using the Cepeda ratios (about 10 to 20 percent of the retention interval at short RIs, falling to 6 to 7 percent at a year), what gap should you target, and which direction is the safer error?
L4.answer: About 11 days for a 35-day interval, about 21 days for 70 days, and about 21 to 23 days for 350 days. Over-spacing is the safer error: the curve rises steeply to the optimum and falls gently after it.
L4.explanation: Note the ratio is not constant - 21/350 is about 6 percent while 11/35 is about 31 percent - so the popular 10 to 20 percent rule is a rounded summary of a ratio that drifts with the retention interval, not a law.

L4.prompt_tpl: Re-reading scores d = {d} in the 2021 meta-analysis yet Dunlosky rates it Low utility. Explain how both can be true.
L4.answer: The meta-analytic d compares re-reading against no treatment, so it is measured against nothing rather than against testing. Dunlosky rates generalizability, and head-to-head re-reading loses badly to practice testing at longer delays. Different comparisons, different questions, no contradiction.
L4.explanation: This is the single most misread table in the learning literature. An effect size is meaningless without its comparison condition, which is why the ordering plus Dunlosky's reasoning matters more than the numbers alone.

# Predicted 1-week recall (confidence):  SSSS 4.8 > SSST 4.2 > STTT 4.0
# The group that performed WORST was the most confident.

# Deslauriers et al. 2019 (Harvard physics RCT, N=149): active learning +0.46 SD

L0.cloze: At one week, four study blocks gave {{c1::40}} percent recall and one study plus three tests gave {{c2::61}} percent - yet the study-only group predicted it would do {{c3::best}}.

concepts.L1: Restudying beats testing at five minutes and loses badly at one week: 40 percent against 61 percent in Roediger and Karpicke's second experiment. The group that performed worst was the most confident about how it would do.
concepts.L2: This is not ignorance you can fix by knowing about it. The signal you use to judge learning is processing fluency, and re-reading raises fluency while doing little for retention, so the feeling of understanding and the fact of it move in opposite directions.
concepts.L3: Deslauriers and colleagues ran the same inversion in a Harvard physics course, 149 students, within-subject randomised: active learning produced a 0.46 standard deviation gain on exams while students rated their perceived learning 0.56 standard deviations lower. Students learn more and feel like they learn less. For tool design: any system letting the learner pick their study mode is pulled toward re-reading, so retrieval must be the default. For you: your sense of whether a session went well is not evidence. The substitutes are objective - first-attempt recall after a day or more, and whether you can produce the answer without the material.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using Roediger and Karpicke's Experiment 2 numbers, compute the SSSS-minus-STTT difference at 5 minutes and at 1 week, and state what the sign change means for a learner judging a session at {t}. Answer with the one-week difference in points.
L4.answer: At 5 minutes SSSS minus STTT is 83 - 71 = +12 points for studying. At 1 week it is 40 - 61 = -21 points, a 33-point swing. A learner judging at the end of a session sees only the +12 and concludes studying works better.
L4.explanation: The testing effect is invisible at short delays and only appears after a day or more, which is exactly why learners disbelieve it. Rowland's moderator table shows the same thing: g = 0.41 under a day, 0.69 at a day or more.

L4.prompt_tpl: Students in the Harvard physics RCT learned {a} SD more and rated their learning {b} SD lower. Explain the mechanism and one design consequence.
L4.answer: They judge learning by fluency, and a smooth lecture feels fluent while effortful active work feels like struggling. Since effort is what produces retention, the felt signal is anti-correlated with the real one. Design consequence: make retrieval the default rather than a setting, and warn the user once that effective sessions feel worse.
L4.explanation: The warning is worth giving even though it does not fully work - Yan, Bjork and Bjork found 60 percent still preferred blocking after being shown the data. It costs nothing and it reframes the discomfort as a signal rather than a failure.

# Rowland 2014 meta-analysis: 159 effect sizes, 61 studies.
# Overall g = 0.50 [0.42, 0.58]; g = 0.66 with matched exposure.

  moderator                        g
  -------------------------------  -----
  with feedback                    0.73
  without feedback                 0.39
  final test = recall              0.49-0.79
  final test = recognition         0.31-0.32
  retention interval >= 1 day      0.69
  initial test performance <= 50%  0.03   <- not significant. zero.
  initial 51-75%                   0.29
  initial > 75%                    0.56
L0.cloze: When initial retrieval success is at or below 50 percent, the testing effect is g = {{c1::0.03}}, statistically indistinguishable from {{c2::zero}}. Feedback raises the effect from 0.39 to {{c3::0.73}}.

concepts.L1: Retrieval only works if it succeeds. Below 50 percent initial success the testing effect is g = 0.03, not distinguishable from zero. Feedback nearly doubles the effect, from 0.39 to 0.73, and recognition formats are worth about half of recall formats.
concepts.L2: The intuition that harder items teach more is wrong past a threshold. Failed retrieval without successful re-encoding is wasted time, so an item you get wrong most of the time is not a challenge to persist with, it is a badly-formed item that needs splitting or more context.
concepts.L3: Four design rules fall out of the moderator table. Always show the answer, because feedback moves g from 0.39 to 0.73 - and do not build delayed-feedback modes, since a 2026 meta-analysis of timing across 51 studies found g = 0.03, a null. Prefer recall over recognition, which earns about 0.31 against 0.49 to 0.79. Make the first review late enough to be effortful but not so late that success collapses. Intercept items you keep failing early rather than at Anki's default of eight lapses, and reformulate: split, add context, or suspend one of two interfering siblings. Matuschak's tractability criterion is the same finding as a design rule.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are getting {p} percent of first attempts right on a deck. Using Rowland's moderator table, estimate the effect size you are getting and say what to change.
L4.answer: At 45 percent, g is about 0.03 - effectively nothing; split the items and add context. At 60 percent, g is about 0.29. At 85 percent, g is about 0.56. Success rate, not difficulty, is what predicts the benefit.
L4.explanation: This inverts the common instinct to make cards harder when learning feels too easy. The evidence says the productive range is high success, and that a deck sitting below half is not training you at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: An item has failed {n} times. Compare persisting, deleting it, and reformulating it, using the moderator table.
L4.answer: Persisting is the worst option: at that success rate the effect is near zero, so the reviews cost time and teach nothing. Reformulate first - split into smaller items, add a disambiguating context tag, or suspend one of two interfering siblings. Delete if the fact fails the value test of being worth more than five minutes of lifetime lookup.
L4.explanation: Anki suspends leeches at eight lapses, which is late and passive. Intercepting at about three and routing to a reformulation flow keeps the failing item from consuming review slots at g near zero while the rest of the deck waits.

concepts.t: Interleaving feels worse and works better

L0.body:
# Kornell & Bjork 2008 (learning painters' styles):
  ~78% classified NEW paintings better after interleaved study
  ~78% believed BLOCKING had been as good or better

# Yan, Bjork & Bjork 2016: after being TOLD 90% do better interleaved,
#   60% still claimed blocking was superior.

# Rohrer 2020 (randomised trial, school maths): interleaving distributes
#   practice AND forces STRATEGY DISCRIMINATION - the student must choose
#   a method rather than only execute a given one.

# Rule: block until each schema exists, then interleave within clusters.
L0.cloze: In Kornell and Bjork's study about {{c1::78}} percent learned better from interleaving and about the same fraction believed {{c2::blocking}} was better. Rohrer's mechanism is {{c3::strategy discrimination}}: choosing the method, not just executing it.

concepts.L1: Mixing topics within a session beats blocking them, and almost everyone believes the opposite. Rohrer's account of why: interleaving forces you to choose a method rather than execute a given one, which is the step blocked practice silently deletes.
concepts.L2: Interleaving is not universally good. Below a threshold of prior knowledge it manufactures failed retrievals, which Rowland shows are worth about zero. The rule is to block until each individual schema exists, then interleave - and to interleave within similar clusters, not across unrelated ones.
concepts.L3: Two findings make interleaving a default the tool enforces rather than a setting. First the size: Kornell and Bjork found around 78 percent classified new paintings better after interleaved study while around 78 percent believed blocking was at least as good. Second the durability: Yan, Bjork and Bjork told participants 90 percent do better interleaved, and 60 percent still said blocking was superior. Preference points the wrong way, so it cannot be the control input. Carvalho and Goldstone give the boundary: interleaving emphasises between-category differences, blocking within-category similarities. Interleave coherence protocols against each other, not against Verilog syntax.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are learning {a} and {b} in the same week. Decide whether to interleave them, and state the prior-knowledge condition on your answer.
L4.answer: Interleave the similar, easily-confused pair with each other, because that is where discrimination is the skill. Do not interleave across the dissimilar pair - there is nothing to discriminate, so it only adds switching cost. And do neither until each item is individually executable, since interleaving a novice produces failed retrievals worth about zero.
L4.explanation: Carvalho and Goldstone's attentional-bias account is the operative rule: interleaving highlights between-category differences, blocking highlights within-category similarities. Match the schedule to which of those you currently need.

L4.prompt_tpl: After being told {p} percent of people learn better from interleaving, {q} percent still preferred blocking. Explain what that implies for how a study tool should be built.
L4.answer: The illusion survives direct instruction, so user preference cannot be the control input for schedule shape. The tool should interleave by default within similarity clusters and gate it on a per-item mastery threshold, while telling the user once that the harder-feeling schedule is the effective one.
L4.explanation: This is the strongest argument in the whole learning literature for an opinionated default. Where a metacognitive illusion is large, documented, and resistant to correction, offering the choice is equivalent to choosing wrong for most users.

# Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006: 94 independent tests, ~8,000 participants.
#   d = 0.65 on goal attainment, OVER AND ABOVE having the goal.

  goal intention:  'I will review every day'                weak
  if-then plan:    'IF it is 07:00 and I have sat down at
                    my desk, THEN I do my reviews'          d = 0.65

# Lally et al. 2010, habit formation in the wild:
#   96 started, 82 finished, only 39 (48%) fit the model at all
#   of those 39: median 66 days to asymptote, RANGE 18-254 days
#   one missed day cost < 0.5 automaticity points, recovered fast
L0.cloze: An if-then plan delegates action initiation to a {{c1::situational cue}} and adds d = {{c2::0.65}} over the goal alone. Lally's median of {{c3::66}} days hides a range of 18 to 254 and applied to fewer than half the participants.

concepts.L1: An if-then plan naming a specific cue - if it is 7 a.m. and I have sat down, then I do my reviews - adds d = 0.65 to goal attainment over the intention alone, across 94 tests and about 8,000 participants. It is the cheapest adherence intervention known.
concepts.L2: The mechanism is delegation, not motivation. Specifying the cue hands action initiation to the situation so it no longer requires a decision, which is why a vague plan with the same goal does nothing. The cue must be a concrete time and place, not a mood.
concepts.L3: The companion finding matters as much. Lally and colleagues tracked habit formation in the wild: of 96 starters, 82 finished and only 39 produced data fitting the automaticity model at all. Among those 39 the median time to 95 percent of asymptote was 66 days with a range of 18 to 254 - a fourteenfold spread - so the quoted 66 days is a median of a minority, not a constant. The most useful result is the smallest: one missed day reduced automaticity by under half a point and recovered quickly. Any product that renders a lapse as a loss is manufacturing a problem the data says does not exist.

L4.prompt_tpl: Rewrite 'I will study {n} minutes a day' as an implementation intention, and explain which part carries the d = 0.65.
L4.answer: If it is 7:30 a.m. and I have sat down with coffee at my desk, then I open the app and do the day's reviews before anything else. The effect comes from the if-clause: a concrete, reliably-encountered situational cue that triggers the action without requiring a decision. Duration is not the operative part.
L4.explanation: Gollwitzer's mechanism is that the cue is encoded so that its occurrence initiates the behaviour automatically. A plan that specifies only the amount, or that names a feeling rather than a situation, has no cue to fire on.

L4.prompt_tpl: Lally reports a median of {m} days with a range of 18 to 254, and only 39 of 82 completers fitting the model. Explain why quoting '{m} days to form a habit' is a misuse.
L4.answer: The median is over the subset whose data fit an asymptotic model at all - fewer than half - and the spread is fourteenfold, so it describes almost nobody in particular. It also measures self-reported automaticity, not behaviour. The defensible claim is that habits take roughly two to eight months and vary enormously between people.
L4.explanation: The finding worth keeping from this study is not the median at all, it is that one missed day costs under half a point and recovers quickly. That is the number that should shape how a tool responds to a lapse.

concepts.L1: Rate your confidence before seeing the answer, then look at the confident-and-wrong cell first. It is the only error class you cannot discover unaided, because in every other cell you already knew something was off.
concepts.L2: Feeling that you understand something is not evidence, and the studies show the correlation can invert: in Roediger and Karpicke the worst-performing group was the most confident. Confidence tracks fluency, and fluency is exactly what re-reading manufactures.

Explain it without the source to someone one step behind; Kobayashi's meta-analysis of 39 studies found teaching after study gives g = 0.48 with teaching expectancy and about -0.02 without, so the expectation at encoding does the work. Name the condition under which the claim stops holding. Pan and Rickard's transfer meta-analysis is the warning: after correcting for publication bias, retrieval often shows no transfer unless elaborated retrieval and adequate success are built in.

L4.prompt_tpl: Across {n} reviews you were confident and wrong on {k} items and unsure and wrong on {m}. Which set do you work on first and why?
L4.answer: The confident-and-wrong set, despite being far smaller. Those items are mismodelled rather than unlearned: you would never have flagged them yourself, and they are load-bearing in reasoning you already do. The unsure-and-wrong set is ordinary study and will be caught by normal review.
L4.explanation: The value of an error signal scales with how unlikely you were to find it unaided. Unsure-and-wrong is self-announcing; confident-and-wrong is silent, which is exactly why it survives and propagates into work you do downstream.

L4.prompt_tpl: Kobayashi found teaching after study gives g = {a} with teaching expectancy and about {b} without. Explain what that implies about when the benefit is produced.
L4.answer: The benefit comes at encoding, not at teaching. Expecting to explain changes how you process the material - you look for structure, gaps and examples - so teaching without that expectation adds essentially nothing. Practically: decide before you study that you will have to explain it.
L4.explanation: This makes the intervention nearly free, since it is a framing rather than an activity. It is also why 'explain it to a rubber duck' works when you commit in advance and does little when bolted on afterwards.

concepts.L1: Mentorship is not requested, it accretes. The unit is a specific question with your attempt attached, followed by actually doing the suggested thing and reporting the result. Do that three times and you have a mentor without either of you naming it.
concepts.L2: The open-ended ask fails for a structural reason: it transfers the whole cost of scoping onto the person you are asking. A specific question with your prior attempt attached costs them minutes and gives them the pleasure of being useful, which is what makes it repeatable.
concepts.L3: A named senior mentor or an active feedback community was one of the four inputs common to every documented fast transition, and it is the one solitary study cannot substitute for. The mechanism is error correction on things you cannot see: you can self-teach facts, but not the taste that tells you a result is suspicious. Communities beat individuals as a starting point because cost per person is lower and latency shorter - EleutherAI's paper records people with minimal background becoming core contributors within weeks in exactly that setting. Public artifacts make you legible enough to be helped: a repo can be judged in five minutes, an ambition cannot.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare two opening messages to a researcher whose work you admire: a request to be mentored, and '{q}'. Explain the asymmetry in cost.

q: I reproduced your Figure 3 and got 68.1 against your 71.4, here is my config - what am I likely missing?
I tried your method on a different dataset and the gain vanished, here is the repo - is that expected?

L4.answer: The first asks them to scope an open-ended relationship, which costs them thinking they have no time for. The second costs a few minutes, is interesting to them because it is about their own work, and creates a natural next exchange. Cost per reply is what determines whether there is a second one.
L4.explanation: The specific message also demonstrates competence without claiming it. A reproduction attempt with a config attached says more about what you can do than any self-description could, and it gives the other person something concrete to respond to.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why joining an active community can outperform finding a single mentor for someone {s}.

s: in a different time zone from their target labs

L4.answer: Lower cost per person, shorter latency, many possible responders, and no single point of failure if one person is busy. Communities also produce public artifacts by default, which was one of the four inputs common to every documented fast transition. A single mentor is higher bandwidth but harder to obtain and easier to lose.
L4.explanation: EleutherAI is the documented case: software engineers and hobbyists with non-traditional backgrounds became core contributors within weeks, with shared compute and constant feedback. The community supplied both the mentorship and the artifact channel.

concepts.L1: Mentorship is advice given to you; sponsorship is advocacy for you in rooms you are not in. Sponsorship is what converts competence into opportunity, and it is much rarer because it costs the sponsor reputation rather than time.
concepts.L2: You cannot ask for sponsorship the way you ask for advice, because a sponsor is staking their own credibility on you. What you can do is make sponsoring you cheap and safe: legible, verifiable work, and a track record of doing what you said you would do.
concepts.L3: The career research is blunt about how much advancement is allocated rather than earned. Larson found roughly two-thirds of staff-plus engineers promoted internally and a third having to change companies, opportunity unevenly distributed across teams, and engineers citing not being in the room where decisions happen. Headquarters staff get more visibility, a structural tax on anyone outside an HQ city. Reilly's Being Glue documents the complement: coordination and mentoring work is systematically unrewarded, with committees answering that you did not produce much code. Public artifacts are the one lever outside this system entirely.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your manager gives excellent advice but never proposes you for visible work. Name what is missing, and give {n} concrete actions that do not involve asking for a promotion.
L4.answer: Sponsorship, not mentorship. Actions: make your work legible in writing where others can see it, volunteer for a scoped project with a visible outcome rather than glue work, and build a public artifact that gives someone outside your reporting line a reason to advocate for you. Ask your manager what would make advocating for you easy.
L4.explanation: The last question is the one that converts the relationship, because it makes the cost explicit and lets them tell you the actual blocker. It also distinguishes a manager who will not sponsor from one who does not know how.

L4.prompt_tpl: Larson found about {a} of staff-plus engineers were promoted internally and about {b} had to change companies. Explain what that implies about treating a title as a measure of skill.
L4.answer: A third of people at that level could not get the title where they were, so the title tracks organisational opportunity and sponsorship as much as capability. It is a joint function of your work, your employer's scope, and someone advocating for you - which means a missing title is weak evidence about skill, in both directions.
L4.explanation: The practical consequence is that employer choice is part of the plan rather than a detail, since a company with no problems at a given scope cannot recognise work at that scope no matter how good you are.

# MATS: 12 weeks, plus a 6-12 month extension.
  631 researchers to date, 220+ papers, 19,000+ citations
  75% of alumni now work in AI alignment, transparency or security
  10% co-founded safety orgs (Apollo Research, Timaeus, Poseidon)

# Anthropic Fellows: 4 months, stipend about USD 3,850 per week,
#   compute about USD 15,000 per month, an Anthropic mentor.
  stated: 'You don't need a PhD, prior ML experience, or published papers.'
  first cohort: 80%+ produced papers; 40%+ joined Anthropic

# Neither publishes an acceptance rate. Outcomes are self-reported.
L0.cloze: MATS reports {{c1::75}} percent of its 631 alumni now working in the field. Anthropic Fellows states you do not need a PhD, prior ML experience or {{c2::published papers}}, and over {{c3::40}} percent of the first cohort joined full-time.

concepts.L1: MATS and the Anthropic Fellows Program are the best-evidenced accelerants available: MATS reports 631 participants, 220-plus papers and 75 percent of alumni now working in the field; Anthropic reports over 80 percent of its first cohort producing papers and over 40 percent hired.
concepts.L2: They do not select for credentials - Anthropic states explicitly that no PhD, prior ML experience or publications are required. They select for evidence that you can do research: strong Python, comfort with ambiguity, fast learning, and something public you actually finished.
concepts.L3: Read the outcome numbers with the selection effect in view. Neither programme publishes an acceptance rate or applicant count and both figures are self-reported, so much of that 75 percent reflects who was admitted rather than what the programme added. Granting that, these are still the strongest outcome data available - far better documented than the bootcamp sector. A strong application contains a finished public artifact with a number in it, an honest account of a project that failed, a specific research direction rather than a general interest, and evidence you work unsupervised. Applying is high expected value precisely because the stated bar is behavioural.

L4.prompt_tpl: MATS reports {n} participants and that {p} percent of alumni now work in the field. About how many people is that, and name two reasons the number overstates the programme's causal effect. Answer with the number of people.
L4.answer: About 473 people, from 0.75 times 631. It overstates the causal effect because participants are selected competitively from an already-strong pool, and because the figure is self-reported by the programme with no control group and no published acceptance rate.
L4.explanation: Selection effects are the standard confound in every programme outcome statistic. The right comparison would be against similar applicants who were rejected, which nobody publishes, so treat the number as an upper bound on the programme's contribution.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {w} weeks and no publications, and want the strongest possible fellowship application. Rank a reproduction with an ablation, a novel side project, and an extra online course.
L4.answer: Reproduction with an ablation first: it is verifiable against a published number and demonstrates measurement, not just building. Novel side project second: real evidence but the reader must evaluate both problem choice and execution. The course last and distantly - certificates without artifacts appear in no hiring account in the research.
L4.explanation: Anthropic's careers page asks for independent research, blog posts or open-source contributions, and states that about half its technical staff had no prior ML experience. The selection signal is demonstrated work, and reproductions are the cheapest demonstrated work that a stranger can check.
